name: David Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the political reporter for a commercial radio group's regional news hub, which means I write and read the hourly bulletins and cover the council, the local MPs and anything at the town hall. I'm in at five, and I use AI every day to pull overnight council papers together, draft bulletin scripts and check figures before I read them out. Then it's out to interviews with a recorder, and back in to cut audio. I enjoy the chase and the live microphone; I don't enjoy the five o'clock alarm or the pay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside the hub.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my younger brother, who's at college training to be a plumber. Our parents live across town; my dad drove buses for thirty years and my mum's a school cook. Money's tight, I've got maybe two weeks of rent saved, and I'm paying off a laptop I bought on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a decent tool if you know how to use it. People who dismissed AI or hyped AI were both wrong. I'd say it on the hub's social pages, probably with a quick example of a bulletin it helped me check. I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit uneasy. The radio group has already merged three local stations into one hub, and they could merge again. But in this picture my AI skills make me a bit quicker than the others, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep sharpening my tools. I'd start a small weekly council newsletter on the side, paid for by a couple of local businesses advertising. I'd pay off the laptop before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. It's the money more than the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which businesses would advertise in a council newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Estate agents, a solicitor or two, maybe the builders' merchant, because they all care about planning decisions. I'd ask for fifty pounds a month each to start. Five of them would cover my phone bill and then some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about the newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say good, be your own boss, he always wanted that and never managed it. My mum would ask if I'm sleeping enough. Both fair points.

say: AI is a **decent tool** if you know how to use it.
People who dismissed it or **hyped** it were both wrong, he'd post.
think: He's **a bit uneasy**, as the radio group has already merged three stations into one hub.
His **AI skills** make him quicker than others, which helps here.
do: Keep sharpening his **AI tools** for bulletins and checks.
Start a **weekly council newsletter** paid for by local advertisers.
Pay off the **laptop credit** before anything else.
feel: **Uneasy** but in control, worried more about money than the job.
S0.quote: People who dismissed AI or hyped AI were both wrong.
fieldNote: His **free-market** instinct shows in the newsletter idea funded by local firms.
Debt on a **laptop** is a small but real strain.
Feels his job is **reasonably safe** here because of his AI skills.

steps.text: Use AI daily to draft and fact-check radio bulletin scripts
Launch a weekly council newsletter funded by local advertisers
Pay off the laptop credit before other spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for local news to get leaner and better, and the people who adapt will be fine. I'd also say listeners will still want a real voice they trust on the radio. I'd be upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the hourly bulletins are an easy target. An AI voice can read the news now, and the radio group would love to drop the presenters on the early shifts. I'd probably keep a job for a while, but on fewer shifts, and I'm on the early shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the council newsletter into a proper business, adding a short podcast and maybe a second town. I'd offer to build the hub's AI bulletin system so I'm the person running it rather than being replaced. I'd also save every bit of newsletter money and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an exciting kind of anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who adapt will be fine. What about the ones who don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel for them, honestly. A couple of the older presenters at the hub hate computers and they've got families. I'd try to help them, but I don't think it's the station's job to keep paying people for work that isn't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the hub to run the newsletter full time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, not with two weeks of rent saved. I'd want the newsletter covering my rent for six months first. Then I'd jump.

say: This is a chance for local news to get **leaner and better**.
Listeners will still want **a real voice** they trust on the radio.
think: The **hourly bulletins** are an easy target, since AI voices can read news now.
He'd likely keep a job but on **fewer shifts**, starting with early ones.
do: Grow the council newsletter into a **business** with a podcast and second town.
Offer to build the hub's **AI bulletin system** himself.
feel: **Anxious**, but an exciting kind of anxious.
S1.quote: An AI voice can read the news now, and the radio group would love to drop the presenters on the early shifts.
fieldNote: Expects **fewer shifts** at the hub, so anxious despite his upbeat tone.
Free-market view: not the station's job to **pay for work** not needed.
Sets a clear **six-month rule** before quitting for his own business.

steps.text: Add a short podcast and a second town to the newsletter
Offer to build the radio hub's AI bulletin system
Bank all newsletter income untouched for six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and local businesses will have to carry each other through this, because it's too fast for anyone to plan. I'd say government should get out of the way of people starting new things. I'd say it on air, if I still had a slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my radio job goes by 2028 and so does most of the newsletter. If AGI can do any thinking work, it can write a council newsletter too. The only thing I'd have is my face and my name locally, and the trust people put in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those two years I'd go out and meet every councillor, business owner and community group I can, so my name means something when the machines arrive. I'd turn the newsletter into local events, debates and public meetings, things that need a person in the room. I'd also help my brother finish his plumbing course, because his trade has until robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Even for me, two years is a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your brother's trade buys time. Would you consider plumbing yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes, if the events thing didn't work. My brother could teach me the basics. I'd rather do that than sit at home on benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, which I mostly use for interviews. Then any eating out. I'd keep the phone and the broadband, because that's the business.

say: **Families** and **local businesses** will have to carry each other through this.
Government should get **out of the way** of people starting new things.
think: His radio job and most of the **newsletter** go by 2028.
All he'd have left is his **local name** and the trust people put in it.
do: Meet every **councillor** and community group in two years to build his name.
Turn the newsletter into **local events** and public debates.
Help his brother finish the **plumbing course** before robots arrive around 2031.
feel: **Alarmed**: even for him, two years is a shock.
S2.quote: The only thing I'd have is my face and my name locally, and the trust people put in it.
fieldNote: Even this **adaptive** reporter expects to lose most income within two years.
Pivots to **in-person** events, the part of his work that needs a person.
Sees his brother's **trade** as a family hedge through the robot gap.

steps.text: Run paid local debates and public meetings instead of a newsletter
Help his brother pay for and finish his plumbing course
Sell the car and stop eating out
Learn basic plumbing from his brother as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people who start preparing now will be glad they did. I'd encourage young people to learn trades and to be enterprising. I'd say it on my podcast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me time to turn the newsletter and events into a proper local media business. My radio job probably goes by 2031, maybe earlier. But I'd have a business with a name, some savings and local advertisers who know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd register the business, sign up ten local advertisers and start monthly public debates. I'd keep the hub job for steady pay until the business covered my rent for six months. I'd also learn to film and edit video properly, since people will want to see real faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more driven than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a local media business exactly what AGI would do better and cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For writing, yes, completely. But people will still want to come to a hall and shout at a councillor in person, and somebody has to run that. I'd use AI for the paperwork and do the people part myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about you leaving a salaried job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say go for it, and then ask if I'd paid my brother's course fees yet. He drove buses so we wouldn't have to worry about money. I'd want to make that count.

say: Five years is a **fair warning**, and starting now pays off.
Young people should learn **trades** and be enterprising.
think: Five years gives time to build a **local media business** with events.
His **radio job** probably goes by 2031, maybe earlier.
do: Register the business and sign up **ten local advertisers**.
Keep the **hub job** until the business covers six months' rent.
Learn to film and edit **video** properly.
S3.quote: People will still want to come to a hall and shout at a councillor in person, and somebody has to run that.
fieldNote: Answers the challenge with a split: **AI for paperwork**, people for the rest.
His dad's years as a **bus driver** shape his sense of duty.
Still expects to lose the **radio job**, so anxiety stays.

steps.text: Register a local media business and sign ten advertisers
Run monthly public debates with councillors
Keep the radio hub job until savings cover six months' rent
Learn video filming and editing for the business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone willing to work and learn can make it through. I'd say local enterprise will matter more than ever. I'd be quite optimistic in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel mostly good about this one. Ten years is enough to build a local media business slowly and properly, and maybe hire a couple of people. I'd be thirty-seven, which is a good age to be running something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hub job for three or four years and grow the newsletter and events steadily. I'd save towards three months of rent, then six. I'd probably also think about settling down, maybe marrying, once the business was steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at times, but mostly hopeful. I like having a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big tech firms taking all the local advertising, like they did with the papers. If that happened, I'd need events and loyalty more than ads. I'd plan for it from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother to finish his plumbing course and learn the business side too. A trade plus knowing how to run a business is the best bet I can think of.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and anyone willing to work and learn can make it.
**Local enterprise** will matter more than ever.
think: He'd feel **mostly good**, with time to build a business slowly.
At **thirty-seven** he could be running something of his own.
do: Keep the **hub job** for three or four years while growing the business.
Save towards **three months** of rent, then six.
Think about **marrying** once the business is steady.
feel: **Uneasy** at times but mostly hopeful, thanks to the long runway.
S4.quote: A trade plus knowing how to run a business is the best bet I can think of.
fieldNote: The long runway suits his **enterprising** nature, so mood eases.
Still wary of **big tech** taking local advertising, as with papers.
Advice to his **brother** mirrors his own plan: skill plus business.

steps.text: Keep the radio hub job for three or four years
Grow the council newsletter and public events steadily
Save three months of rent, then six
Plan to marry once the business is steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough to build anything that lasts. What would help is fewer rules and lower costs for starting a small business, and cheap loans for young people with a real plan. Also adult apprenticeships, for people like me who might need a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how important trust is going to be. When anything can be faked, a local reporter people have met and can shout at in the supermarket is worth more, not less. I'd bet my career on that.

headlineQuote: When anything can be faked, a local reporter people have met and can shout at in the supermarket is worth more, not less.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old political reporter** at a commercial radio news hub, sharing a flat with his younger brother.
He uses **AI daily**, favours free markets and family, and wants to build his own local media business.
He's **uneasy** in AI Plateau and AGI by 2036, but **alarmed** under AGI by 2028.
His plan rests on **local trust**: a council newsletter, public debates and his brother's plumbing trade as a family hedge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to build anything lasting.
whatWouldHelp: **Fewer rules** and cheap loans for young people starting businesses.
**Adult apprenticeships** for those who need a trade.
